description_full: Grindr Inc. operates a social networking and dating application for the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer (LGBTQ) communities worldwide. It manages and operates Grindr platform, a social networking platform serving and addressing the needs of gay, bisexual, and sexually explorative adults. It also offers Grindr as the Global Gayborhood in Your Pocket brand. In addition, the company provides ad-supported service and a premium subscription version. Grindr Inc. was founded in 2009 and is headquartered in West Hollywood, California.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 172 people. Revenue per employee of $2.6M ranks in the top quartile among Technology peers, improving at 31%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $818K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $317K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (10/10).
financial_summary: Grindr Inc. is a mid-cap technology business with a $2.4B market cap on $440M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +31% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +7.3pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 31% against a 8% cost of capital — a 22-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $141M in free cash flow — roughly 32 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.49× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -8.8% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.3× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.3×.

Management returns a meaningful 18.7% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and stock-based comp at 12% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insiders hold 82% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

sect: Its 29% operating margin runs 22pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 27% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 44% and a beta of 0.87, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.69 vs 5y 0.18), so read it loosely.
About $22.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 87% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 28% below its DCF fair value of $18.78, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 41%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $7.58 to $42.56 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/FCF 17.1 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.6% (vs the 8% bar).

The price implies 13.7% annual cash-flow growth, 9pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 31% clears the cost of capital of 8.5% by 22pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.79).
It converts 32% of revenue into free cash flow, or 20% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 1.49x, but high accruals (-8.8% of assets).
ROE of 202% is amplified by 11.3x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 11.1% of revenue on R&D and 12.4% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.3x net debt to EBITDA ($87.0M of cash against $395.9M of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.3x.
Goodwill makes up 52% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 31.1% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 24% of profits supports about 7.2% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs only 0.1x depreciation (0.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
It has missed earnings estimates by 6.0% on average.
own: Insiders own 82.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 25%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (19 sales, net $31.1M sold).
It returns 18.7% a year to shareholders (18.7% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 2.2% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
Short interest is elevated at 17.4% of the float, 4.6 days to cover.
people: With about 172 employees, each generates about $2.6M of revenue, 6.9x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 31.1% a year.
That works out to $818K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.9M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
